tweets.text:
In 2012 a 26-year-old dropout sold a location app that never caught on for $43.4 million, and the deal became step one toward OpenAI. Silicon Valley never called it a hit: after seven years and over $30 million raised, the app was sold and shut down.

His name was Sam Altman, and in startups he was an original - a founder in Y Combinator's first batch of just 8 companies, who left Stanford at 19 to build it. At 23 he demoed the app on Apple's stage at WWDC 2008.

Then he did something no one asked for. He pointed the startup playbook at artificial intelligence.

Small inputs: one location app and a seat in that first batch. It raised over $30 million and sold for $43.4 million in March 2012. Most people saw a stalled app; he saw seven years of reps.

A month later he co-founded Hydrazine Capital with his brother Jack. In 2014 he became president of Y Combinator. In 2015 he co-founded OpenAI.

The payoff never came from the exit price. It came from the reps.

The rule behind it is one line:

Judge a founder by the next move, not the last exit.

Old logic says a $43.4 million sale of a stalled app is a failure. Compounding logic says it is tuition - because the lessons carry into the next company.

Then Altman went further. By 2019 he stepped back from Y Combinator to focus on OpenAI full time. The stage changed from a WWDC keynote to global AI, but the habit stayed the same: ship early, learn in public.

He never got the hit app. He got the education that made everything after it possible.

quoted_tweet.text:
This is Sam Altman at 25, pitching Loopt to a stranger in a diner.

It is strange to watch now, given he runs one of the most influential companies in the world.

Loopt was a location sharing app. Nobody thinks about it when they think of Sam Altman today.

Makes you wonder how many founders right now are living their own Loopt era.

The thing they are building may never be the thing they get known for. It might just be the company that teaches them how to sell, how to hire, how to raise money, and how to keep going long enough to eventually find the one that sticks.

But in the moment, it looks like a kid trying to explain a weird location app to a stranger over lunch.
